claims.shared_description: At the coupled tagmentation abstraction, adapter-loaded Tn5 fragments genomic DNA within chromatin and transfers sequencing-adapter sequences, producing tagged fragments that can enter library amplification. The shared transformation is DNA fragmentation plus adapter tagging; the transposome supplies the adapter payload and catalysis, while genomic DNA is the eventual readout carrier.
claims.difference: Left: Tn5 interrogates accessible DNA in native chromatin from unfixed nuclei, without chromatin immunoprecipitation; less accessible chromatin reduces insertion probability. Right: Tn5 acts on already fragmented, immunoprecipitated chromatin retained on beads, with subsequent reverse-crosslinking reported in Methods. Antibody selection of a protein or histone modification precedes tagging. Thus neither the substrate preparation nor the selection principle is shared. The left drawing retains nucleosome-associated pieces after tagging; the right free-looking 'Fragmented and primed' line is an abstraction of tagged DNA still in bead-bound chromatin, not evidence that DNA was deproteinized before tagmentation. Both later recover and amplify DNA, but from these different physical inputs.
claims.consequence: Left authors report preferential production of amplifiable fragments at open chromatin, making insertion positions and insert lengths informative about accessibility and chromatin organization. Right authors retain the antibody-selected genomic population, with antibody quality limiting applicability. They proposed that retained chromatin proteins protect against excessive tagmentation and observed robustness over a 25-fold transposase-concentration range in their tested ChIPmentation experiments. That observation does not isolate protein protection as its cause and is not a demonstration that ChIPmentation is more robust than ATAC-seq.
claims.rationale: The left paper explicitly establishes simultaneous fragmentation and adapter tagging, and the right paper explicitly applies tagmentation to immunoprecipitated bead-bound chromatin. This supports the same specified DNA transformation despite different preparation, carrier attachment and selection. The relation rests on the transformation and substrate context, rather than the enzyme name alone; it does not align accessibility selection with antibody capture.

left_evidence.quote: Hyperactive Tn5 transposase10,11, loaded in vitro with adapters for high-throughput DNA sequencing, can simultaneously fragment and tag a genome with sequencing adapters (previously described as “tagmentation”11).

Because transposons have been shown to integrate into active regulatory elements in vivo12, we hypothesized that transposition by purified Tn5, a prokaryotic transposase, on small numbers of unfixed eukaryotic nuclei would interrogate regions of accessible chromatin.

ATAC-seq uses Tn5 transposase to integrate its adapter payload into regions of accessible chromatin, whereas steric hindrance less accessible chromatin makes transposition less probable. Therefore, amplifiable DNA fragments suitable for high-throughput sequencing are preferentially generated at locations of open chromatin (Fig 1a).
These insights are derived from both the position of insertion and the distribution of insert lengths captured during the transposition reaction.

right_evidence.quote: The development of a hyperactive Tn5 transposase that enables simultaneous DNA fragmentation and adapter tagging (“tagmentation”) presents an opportunity for faster and more sensitive library preparation from purified DNA3.
Here, we demonstrate tagmentation of immunoprecipitated chromatin in a robust one-step reaction performed directly on bead-bound chromatin.

Given that ChIPmentation involves tagmentation of fragmented chromatin instead of purified ChIP DNA, we also investigated whether the tagmentation patterns correlate with local chromatin structure as described for ATAC-seq4.

We reasoned that performing tagmentation directly on the immunoprecipitated and bead-bound chromatin would allow chromatin proteins to protect the DNA from excessive tagmentation. Our ChIPmentation protocol (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1 and Online Methods) was indeed robust over a 25-fold difference in transposase concentrations according to five different metrics: measured size distribution of ChIPmentation libraries (Supplementary Fig. 3), size distribution inferred from paired-end sequencing reads (Fig. 1b), read mapping performance (Fig. 1c), concordance between sequencing profiles (Fig. 1d), and signal correlations (Fig. 1e).
Afterward, the chosen ChIP protocol was resumed with the final bead wash, elution from beads, reverse-crosslinking, and DNA purification.
Nevertheless, as with every ChIP approach, low-input ChIPmentation depends on antibody quality and may not be feasible for all histone marks and transcription factors.

unresolved: The matching reaction does not establish identical accessible genomic populations, safe interchange of substrates or reaction conditions, equal insertion bias, equal sensitivity, or equal performance.

The unbound-looking and faded chromatin icons on the right have no separately retained output or bifurcating material flow in the reviewed graph. Their fate is not assigned a new branch, and the purified-ChIP-DNA comparator discussed in the paper is not imported into this diagram.

The colored adapter marks do not specify complete adapter sequences, strand polarities or terminal chemistry. Exact end-structure equivalence is not established and is unnecessary for this qualified tagmentation correspondence.

claims.shared_description: The complete combined recovery/amplification blocks serve a comparable function: turn the respective tagmented chromatin-derived material into a purified, amplified genomic DNA library carrying adapter-associated priming handles. Library DNA preserves genomic origins, but those origins reflect different upstream selection histories.
claims.difference: Left: the standard implementation purifies immediately after transposition and amplifies with NEBnext and custom Nextera primers; qPCR guides stopping before saturation. The authors avoid size selection to maximize library complexity. Their low-cell-number implementation omits the pre-PCR Minelute purification, showing that the broad diagram block is not a universal fixed sequence of handling steps. Right: the combined block must recover DNA after bead-bound tagmentation through bead elution, reverse-crosslinking and purification, followed by KAPA-based enrichment, qPCR-based cycle estimation and SPRI size selection removing long fragments above 600 bp. Left library composition primarily samples accessible chromatin; right library composition retains the history of antibody selection after protein association and bead attachment are removed.
claims.consequence: Both yield DNA suitable for sequencing, but matching endpoint labels do not imply identical recovery chemistry, fragment-length representation or quantitative recovery. The left authors' complexity rationale explains their decision to avoid size selection; the right Methods document length selection. These passages do not measure a causal advantage of either choice over the other method, and they do not establish equal library complexity or amplification bias.
claims.rationale: This claim compares the functions of the entire broad blocks. PCR copying is explicitly present in both, but that common component does not establish a common mechanism for the whole recovery ensemble, especially release and crosslink reversal on the right. Therefore the block-level relation is shared_purpose, without implying chemical equivalence. The primer adoption inside these same unsplit blocks is separately supported in c3.

left_evidence.quote: Directly following transposition the sample was purified using a Qiagen Minelute kit.
PCR: Following purification, we amplified library fragments using 1x NEBnext PCR master mix and 1.25 μM of custom Nextera PCR primers 1 and 2 (see table below), using the following PCR conditions:
To reduce GC and size bias in our PCR we monitored the PCR reaction using qPCR in order to stop amplification prior to saturation.
Also, we eliminated the Qiagen Minelute purification prior to PCR and instead took the 5 μL reaction immediately after transposition directly into the 50 μL PCR.
During the ATAC-seq protocol, we chose to avoid a size selection step to maximize the library complexity.
ATAC-seq is an information rich assay, allowing simultaneous interrogation of factor occupancy, nucleosome positions in regulatory sites, and chromatin accessibility genome-wide.

right_evidence.quote: Afterward, the chosen ChIP protocol was resumed with the final bead wash, elution from beads, reverse-crosslinking, and DNA purification.

Final enrichment of the libraries was performed in a 50 μl reaction using 0.75 μM primers and 25 μl 2x KAPA HiFi HotStart ReadyMix. Libraries were amplified for N cycles, where N is equal to the rounded-up Cq value determined in the qPCR reaction.

Enriched libraries were purified with size-selection using SPRI AMPure XP beads at a beads-to-sample ratio of 0.7:1 to remove long fragments (>600 bp), recovering the remaining DNA in the reaction using a beads-to-sample ratio of 2:1.
ChIP-seq combines chromatin immunoprecipitation with next generation sequencing in order to measure the genome-wide distribution of chromatin proteins and their posttranslational modifications1.

unresolved: The blocks do not expose separate operations for elution, crosslink reversal, cleanup, amplification or length selection. An operation-level comparison isolating any one of those processes would require a finer extraction; no such internal IDs are invented here. Paper annotations are sufficient for the present whole-block functional comparison.

Neither the identical caption nor the shared use of PCR establishes that the complete blocks can be substituted across the two input materials. Differences in recovery loss and amplification bias are not quantified in a matched comparison by these passages.

claims.shared_description: Within the existing combined purification/amplification blocks, ChIPmentation explicitly adopts the custom Nextera primer implementation described for ATAC-seq to prepare/amplify the tagged DNA library. This is a historical claim about that primer component, not inheritance of the entire block or assay.
claims.difference: Left: the original ATAC-seq paper independently reports using custom Nextera PCR primers 1 and 2 with NEBnext after purification of transposed nuclear DNA. Right: the ChIPmentation paper explicitly attributes its custom Nextera primers to ATAC-seq while using KAPA enrichment on recovered ChIPmentation DNA. Its bead recovery, crosslink reversal, cycle estimation and size selection remain its own reported implementation context. Adoption of the primer component does not establish adoption of the left substrate preparation or accessibility-selection architecture.
claims.consequence: The citation establishes an implemented transfer of the library-amplification primer component into the later workflow. Neither paper isolates a performance benefit caused by that transfer, and it does not imply identical complete adapters, cycling behavior, library representation or measured biological output.
claims.rationale: The right Online Methods amplification section states 'as described for ATAC-seq4'; reference 4 in the right bibliography resolves to Buenrostro et al., PMID 24097267, the registered left original paper. The left Methods independently describe the cited custom-primer implementation. This combination satisfies component_adoption and supplies direction through explicit attribution, rather than publication dates or a shared Tn5 label. The exact existing broad Operation IDs are used to attach this qualified component annotation; no primer-only operation is created.

Hyperactive Tn5 transposase10,11, loaded in vitro with adapters for high-throughput DNA sequencing, can simultaneously fragment and tag a genome with sequencing adapters (previously described as “tagmentation”11).

right_evidence.quote: Library preparation was performed using custom Nextera primers as described for ATAC-seq4.
Final enrichment of the libraries was performed in a 50 μl reaction using 0.75 μM primers and 25 μl 2x KAPA HiFi HotStart ReadyMix.

The development of a hyperactive Tn5 transposase that enables simultaneous DNA fragmentation and adapter tagging (“tagmentation”) presents an opportunity for faster and more sensitive library preparation from purified DNA3. Furthermore, tagmentation of intact chromatin followed by sequencing (ATAC-seq) was shown to yield open chromatin profiles comparable to those obtained by DNase-seq4. In contrast, this technique has not yet been adapted for ChIP-seq sample preparation.

unresolved: No method_development relation for the complete ATAC-seq assay architecture is established here. The right introduction frames extension of chromatin tagmentation to ChIP, but separately attributes generic tagmentation to Adey et al. (reference 3), also credited as prior tagmentation by the left paper (reference 11). The explicit implementation transfer identified here concerns custom Nextera primers; enzyme reuse and an ATAC citation alone do not establish whole-assay inheritance.
The separate ATAC-seq experiment described in the right paper is an adapted open-chromatin control for its analyses, not evidence that ChIPmentation itself runs the complete ATAC-seq workflow.
Complete primer/adaptor sequence identity is not reconstructed from the diagrams' colored ends. The historical conclusion is limited to the implementation explicitly attributed by the authors.

claims.shared_description: The papers support a documented comparison of local Tn5 insertion/footprint information carried by libraries produced by the connected tagmentation-to-library groups. Both can carry information about protein-associated protection, but their genomic sampling and interpretation differ. This relation records the published methodological comparison; sequencing and computational analysis remain downstream annotations beyond these diagrams' library endpoints.
claims.difference: Left: the original ATAC-seq paper demonstrates footprint-based inference of factor occupancy from accessible chromatin, including CTCF in GM12878, and combines insertion data with motif score and evolutionary conservation. Right: ChIPmentation starts this selected group with already immunoprecipitated bead-bound chromatin; its primary readout is target enrichment. The right authors generated ATAC-seq controls with minor adaptations for K562 cells, then compared motif-centered ChIPmentation, ATAC-seq, DNase-seq and naked-genomic-DNA tagmentation signals. They corrected ChIPmentation and ATAC-seq patterns using the naked-DNA background. Thus this was not a comparison of identical input fractions or an unchanged replication of every original ATAC implementation detail.
claims.consequence: The original left paper reports a CTCF protection footprint and occupancy inference concordant with ChIP-seq in its tested cell line. The right authors report that, after correction, ChIPmentation footprints for CTCF and REST resembled ATAC-seq and DNase-seq footprints, while none of those methods detected footprints for GATA1 and PU.1 in that analysis. They also observed patterns in naked-DNA libraries and attributed part of the signal to transposase sequence bias. These are limited observed similarities and an author interpretation of bias, not evidence of general assay equivalence, universal factor occupancy detection or equal performance.
claims.rationale: The right paper explicitly asks whether fragmented-chromatin tagmentation patterns track local structure as described for ATAC-seq, reports the comparative result, and specifies the compared signals and background normalization. The left paper independently establishes the referenced ATAC footprint readout. This is a documented comparison rather than an ancestry claim. The full group boundaries retain native nuclear chromatin on the left versus antibody-selected bead-bound chromatin and a Tn5 reagent input on the right; neither group absorbs a new analysis operation or the right upstream ChIP operation.

left_evidence.quote: We reasoned that DNA sequences directly occupied by DNA-binding proteins are protected from transposition; the resulting sequence “footprint” reveals the presence of the DNA-binding protein at each site, analogous to DNase digestion footprints24.

At a specific CTCF binding site on chromosome 1, we observed a clear footprint (a deep notch of ATAC-seq signal), similar to footprints seen by DNase-seq25,26, at the precise location of the CTCF motif that coincides with the summit of the CTCF ChIP-seq signal in GM12878 cells (Fig 4a).

We inferred the CTCF binding probability from motif consensus score, evolutionary conservation, and ATAC-seq insertion data to generate a posterior probability of CTCF binding at all loci (Fig. 4c)27. Results using ATAC-seq closely recapitulate ChIP-seq binding data in this cell line and compare favorably to DNase-based factor occupancy inference (see Supplementary Fig. 9), suggesting that factor occupancy data can be extracted from these ATAC-seq data allowing reconstruction of regulatory networks.

right_evidence.quote: Given that ChIPmentation involves tagmentation of fragmented chromatin instead of purified ChIP DNA, we also investigated whether the tagmentation patterns correlate with local chromatin structure as described for ATAC-seq4.

However, some of these patterns were also present in genome sequencing libraries prepared by tagmentation of purified genomic DNA (Supplementary Fig. 7a), suggesting that they originate in part from DNA sequence biases of the transposase. After bioinformatic correction we observed footprints for CTCF and REST, which resembled those found in ATAC-seq and DNase-seq data, but none of these methods detected footprints for GATA1 and PU.1 (Supplementary Fig. 7b and Online Methods).
Open chromatin mapping was performed using the ATAC-seq method as described4 with minor adaptations for K562 cells.

We retrieved a 400 bp window around each motif and used these windows to count four signals: Tn5 insertion events for ChIPmentation of the respective factor, ATAC-seq hits (5′ position of overlapping reads), DNase-seq cut sites in K562 cells from ENCODE25, and Tn5 insertion sites (5′ position of overlapping reads) for a Nextera whole genome sequencing sample prepared from genomic DNA.
To normalize the ChIPmentation and ATAC-seq signals, we divided the observed value at each position by the exponential of the Nextera background signal at the same position.

unresolved: The registered original full texts and relevant citation contexts were accessible and read. Supplementary figures and the detailed ChIP Supplementary Note referred to in the right main text were not separately available as registered evidence; their underlying figures/protocol variants were not independently inspected. Reported footprint outcomes here rely on the accessible main-text and Online Methods statements.

The current diagrams end at DNA libraries. They can anchor this qualified comparison of reported downstream readouts, but an operation-level alignment of sequencing, insertion-coordinate adjustment, background correction or occupancy inference would require a finer extraction of those missing analysis distinctions. None is added during this run.

Similar corrected aggregate footprints at tested factors do not establish that accessibility profiling substitutes for antibody-based target mapping, or that either assay provides universally accurate footprints.

operation_coverage.explanation: Matches right op_tagment for the specified coupled DNA fragmentation/adapter-tagging mechanism (c1), with native nuclear substrate and accessibility sampling retained as left-specific context. Together with left recovery/amplification it anchors the documented footprint comparison (c4). It is not treated as antibody-mediated chromatin capture.

The unsplit block has a comparable complete library-recovery/amplification function (c2), contains the custom-primer implementation explicitly adopted on the right (c3), and completes the left group producing libraries for the reported readout comparison (c4). Purification and PCR are not assigned new internal IDs.

Unmatched. This operation selects protein- or histone-mark-associated chromatin onto beads before Tn5 tagging. The original left assay inserts adapters into accessible native nuclear chromatin without chromatin immunoprecipitation; accessibility-dependent sampling supplies no equivalent antigen-capture operation. Right paper b00005-b00006 describes its target-mapping and bead-bound context, while left b00008 describes the different accessibility selection principle. The unmatched step is a meaningful methodological difference, not an extraction defect.

Matches the coupled tagmentation mechanism (c1), while its bead-bound, already fragmented and antibody-selected input remains explicit. With right recovery/amplification it anchors the documented footprint comparison (c4). The Tn5 input is a reagent branch; no retained unbound-chromatin or purified-DNA route is inferred from pale icons.

The complete block has a comparable library-production function (c2) and contains the explicitly adopted ATAC custom-primer component (c3), but includes right-specific bead elution and crosslink reversal. It completes the right library group for the documented readout comparison (c4). Its internal recovery and amplification procedures remain annotations, not newly addressable operations.

diagram_adequacy.explanation: The existing two operations suffice for the qualified tagmentation mechanism, broad library-production function, primer-component adoption annotation and whole-group readout comparison. 'Open DNA' describes accessible DNA within native chromatin; the repeated vignette is not an opening operation, and final multiple DNA strokes do not form alternative routes. The original paper supplies the unfixed nuclear context, preferential rather than absolute accessibility sampling, custom-primer implementation, purification variation at low input, and lack of size selection. No finer extraction is required for these claims. Separately addressable purification-versus-PCR comparisons or an operation-level alignment of downstream footprint analysis would require distinctions absent from the current broad block/library endpoint; those narrower questions remain unresolved.

The three existing operations preserve the key additional antibody-selection step and support qualified correspondence of tagmentation and downstream library production. Paper annotations are essential: tagmentation is on already fragmented immunoprecipitated bead-bound chromatin; the free-looking tagged-DNA line remains attached until the combined recovery block; and the pale unattached icon does not define another retained workflow. Elution, reverse-crosslinking, primer adoption and size selection can be explained inside the existing broad block without editing it. The original papers support the recorded claims at this level. Separate operation-level attribution of bead release, crosslink reversal, cleanup and PCR, or alignment of downstream footprint-correction operations, would require finer extraction for those specified unresolved questions, not an executable recipe or redesign during this run.

summary: The reviewed graphs are sufficient with paper annotations for the supported block-level comparison. They share a specified chromatin-DNA tagmentation mechanism, while native-nucleus accessibility sampling on the left differs from fragmented, antibody-selected bead-bound chromatin on the right. Their combined recovery/amplification blocks share a library-production purpose with different recovery and length-selection contexts. The later paper explicitly adopts the earlier custom Nextera primer implementation; this supports component_adoption, not complete ATAC-seq workflow inheritance or a method_development claim. A published corrected-footprint comparison is documented separately from mechanism and history. All five operations receive coverage; right chromatin immunoprecipitation remains unmatched. No states, operations or input graphs were changed. Narrower comparisons of internal recovery processes or downstream analysis operations remain beyond the existing graph granularity.
